relevance.rationale: A physics-side review of the non-Abelian Stokes theorem: the operator form, two path-integral variants, the topologically-nontrivial (knotted-loop) generalisation, a higher-degree-form recipe, and applications to 2d Yang-Mills and Chern-Simons. The corpus's load-bearing non-abelian Stokes is the algebraic Yekutieli multiplicative integral (rem:yekutieli-stokes, sec:yekutieli-mapping-table), so this is not load-bearing. It is nonetheless the closest literature statement of the form the corpus actually writes down in rem:lattice-qcd-from-qou, which asserts Hol(dSigma) as a surface-ordered path-ordered integral of the q-deformed curvature over a Seifert surface with no citation at all. Section 2.3.1 additionally treats the case the corpus needs and the standard statement does not cover: the loop bounding the surface is knotted. Not core because the corpus derives nothing from it -- it would source a statement, not supply a step.

keyResults.statement: In its operator form the non-Abelian Stokes theorem states that the path-ordered holonomy around a closed curve C = boundary(S) equals the surface-ordered exponential of the twisted curvature over S.
keyResults.useForFolio: Sources the surface-ordered-exponential formula that rem:lattice-qcd-from-qou states without a citation.

keyResults.statement: When the loop is knotted the naive surface-ordered form fails; the knotted loop is decomposed into a product of surface factors indexed by the genus of the spanning surface, giving the topologically-nontrivial version of the theorem.
keyResults.useForFolio: The corpus applies non-abelian Stokes to holonomy around knots with a Seifert spanning surface, i.e. exactly the topologically-nontrivial case; this flags that the untwisted statement does not cover it.

proposedActions.rationale: No ref() entry exists; the surface-ordered non-abelian Stokes form used in rem:lattice-qcd-from-qou currently has no source of any kind.

rem:lattice-qcd-from-qou opens with the surface-ordered holonomy formula and cites nothing; the knotted-loop caveat of sec. 2.3.1 is directly relevant since the corpus's spanning surface is a Seifert surface of a knot.
